assist_review_intro: The assistant reads the whole model and reports what looks wrong: elements without a description, ones nothing talks to, apparent duplicates. It is advice, not a verdict — nothing is changed.
assist_review_filter_empty: No findings at this level — tap the badge again to see the rest.

assist_review_dropped: {{count}} finding(s) were discarded for naming elements that are not in the model.
assist_guidance_shared_datastore_why: When several services read and write the same tables, the schema becomes a contract nobody owns. A column one team renames breaks the others at runtime, and the database — not the services — is where the system is actually coupled.
assist_guidance_shared_datastore_look: Check whether one of these services owns this data. If it does, the others should go through it rather than the tables. If none does, the store is probably two stores that were merged by accident.
assist_guidance_god_service_why: One element carrying most of the traffic and most of the responsibilities is where releases queue up: every change touches it, so every team waits on it, and its failure is the whole system's failure.
assist_guidance_god_service_look: Read its own description. If it lists several jobs joined by "and", those are the seams — and they usually follow business capabilities rather than technical layers.
assist_guidance_chatty_coupling_why: Two elements that call each other constantly are one element with a network in the middle: you pay for latency, retries and partial failure, and get none of the independence a boundary is supposed to buy.
assist_guidance_chatty_coupling_look: Look at what actually crosses. If most calls are one side fetching data to make a decision, the decision probably belongs on the other side, and the boundary is drawn in the wrong place.
assist_guidance_single_point_of_failure_: Everything depends on it and nothing stands in front of it: when it is slow the whole system is slow, and when it is down the parts that could have carried on go down with it.
Ask what each caller does when this stops answering. The ones that could degrade instead of failing are where a timeout, a cached fallback or a circuit breaker earns its keep.
assist_guidance_cycle_why: A loop means none of the elements in it can be understood, released or replaced on its own. It also hides well: every hop looks reasonable in isolation, and only the ring is wrong.
assist_guidance_cycle_look: Find the hop carrying the least. It is usually a call that had to be answered where an event could have been published instead, which breaks the ring without moving any responsibility.
assist_guidance_direct_external_access_w: When outside traffic reaches several internal elements directly, each of them has to handle authentication, rate limiting and versioning on its own — and the outside world learns your internal shape, which then cannot change without breaking somebody.
assist_guidance_direct_external_access_l: Check whether these entry points agree on auth and error handling. Where they do not, an entry point in front of them is cheaper than keeping them in step by hand.
assist_guidance_duplication_why: Two elements doing the same job means every change has to be made twice — and eventually is not. The two drift, and the one nobody remembers is the one still serving traffic.
assist_guidance_duplication_look: Compare who calls each of them. The same job with different callers usually means one is an older path that was never removed.
assist_guidance_missing_contract_why: Something calls it, but the model does not say how. The endpoint or the channel is the part a new joiner, a downstream team or an agent actually needs: without it the diagram says who talks, not what is said.
assist_guidance_missing_contract_look: Add the endpoint or the channel with its request and response — or mark the element external, if the contract belongs to somebody else.
assist_guidance_layering_why: A connection that skips a level or points the wrong way makes the model unreadable: the picture stops matching how the system is reasoned about, and every later reader has to be told the exception out loud.
assist_guidance_layering_look: Decide whether the connection is real or a drawing shortcut. If it is real, the element it skips over is probably missing from the model.
assist_guidance_orphaned_why: Nothing calls it and it calls nothing. Either a connection is missing from the model — the common case — or the element is genuinely unused, and the model is showing you dead weight.
assist_guidance_orphaned_look: Ask what triggers it. Scheduled jobs and queue consumers often look orphaned because the thing that starts them was never drawn.

helper_system_purpose: The widest view: your product as one box, the people who use it and the outside systems it talks to.
helper_system_tip_1: Draw your product as a single box. The insides come one level down.
helper_system_tip_2: Add the people who use it — they are part of the picture.
helper_system_tip_3: Add only the outside systems you actually exchange data with.
helper_system_tip_4: Mark anything your team does not own as external.
helper_system_tip_5: Label each arrow with what flows, not with the protocol.
helper_container_purpose: What runs and what stores: the separately deployable apps, services, databases and queues inside your product.
helper_container_tip_1: One box per thing you deploy or run on its own.
helper_container_tip_2: Put the technology on the box — that is what readers come here for.
helper_container_tip_3: Databases, caches and queues are containers too.
helper_container_tip_4: On the arrows write who calls whom, and how: REST, gRPC, events.
helper_container_tip_5: Give boxes that ship together the same group.
helper_component_purpose: The main building blocks inside one container — the parts worth naming when you explain how it works.
helper_component_tip_1: Split by responsibility, not by folder layout.
helper_component_tip_2: Name what it does, not the class it happens to be.
helper_component_tip_3: Add an API endpoint for every contract others depend on.
helper_component_tip_4: Stop where a newcomer stops asking questions.
helper_code_purpose: The last level: the few classes and functions that are worth pinning down in the model.
helper_code_tip_1: Only add code that explains a decision someone would question.
helper_code_tip_2: Paste the signature or the key snippet, not the whole file.
helper_code_tip_3: Keep it attached to the component it belongs to.
helper_code_tip_4: Delete it once the real code has moved on — stale code is worse than none.

onboarding_intro: Browser-based visual editor for software architecture with the C4 model — system context, containers, components and code on one shared model, with live collaboration and project sharing.

tips_tour_welcome_body: A short walkthrough of the editor chrome — left tools, canvas navigation, and the top toolbar. Takes about a minute.
tips_tour_rail_body: Primary editing actions live here: add blocks, export/import the model, and reset. Always pinned to the left of the canvas.
tips_tour_add_body: Create a new C4 element for the current level — system, container, component, or code. The menu adapts to where you are in the hierarchy.
tips_tour_export_body: Download the model as JSON — either the full project or only the current view. Handy for backups and sharing offline.
tips_tour_import_body: Load a previously exported JSON model into this editor. Guest sessions stay in the browser until you sign in.
tips_tour_reset_body: Clear the local model and start over. You’ll get a confirmation before anything is wiped.
tips_tour_nav_body: Double-click a block to drill into the next C4 level. Use the breadcrumbs under the top bar to go back. Right-click a block for highlight, docs, sequences and more.
tips_tour_top_body: Global actions and views live here — help, markdown docs, sequence diagrams, theme, service catalog, Magic flows, and sign-in.
tips_tour_help_body: Opens product documentation: C4 levels, collaboration, and how the editor fits together.
tips_tour_docs_body: Write markdown docs attached to systems, containers, components or code. Open from here or from the badge on a block.
tips_tour_sequence_body: PlantUML sequence editor for containers and components. Also available from the GitBranch badge on a block when diagrams exist.
tips_tour_theme_body: Toggle light and dark mode. Canvas colors and chrome follow this setting.
tips_tour_catalog_body: Browse containers by category (service, gateway, broker, database), search, and jump back to the diagram focused on that element.
tips_tour_flows_body: Cross-service journeys as ordered hops. Open the manager from here, play a flow back on the diagram, and mark async fan-out as parallel branches.
tips_tour_signin_body: Create an account to save cloud projects, share with teammates, and keep work across devices. Local editing works without signing in.
tips_tour_done_body: Try the starter template if you haven’t — double-click blocks to explore levels, and use the left rail to add your own elements.
landing_subheadline: Draw system context, containers, components and code. Attach the docs, sequence diagrams and API contracts to the elements they belong to. Serve the whole thing to Cursor or Claude Code over MCP.
landing_cta_local_hint: free · no account · runs in this browser · export any time
landing_trust_title: Your architecture, on terms you can check
landing_trust_body: An architecture model is a map of everything you run, which makes “where does it live?” the first fair question about a tool like this. Three answers, all of them verifiable.
landing_trust_1_title: It stays where you put it
landing_trust_1_body: Without an account the model never leaves your browser. With one it lives on servers in the Netherlands, inside the EU, and so do the backups.
landing_trust_2_title: You can take it with you
landing_trust_2_body: The whole model exports as JSON, and a container’s endpoints as an OpenAPI document — any time, without asking us. Nothing here is a one-way door.
landing_trust_3_title: The agent gets in only if you let it
landing_trust_3_body: MCP access needs a personal token you issue yourself, scoped to your projects. Revoke it and the access ends that moment.
landing_demo_link: Open a real model, no account needed
landing_faq_title: Answered before you have to ask
projects_signed_out: Sign in to see your projects.
projects_tree_hint: Double-click to open · drag onto a folder to move
projects_select_hint: Pick a project to see what it holds.
projects_sign_in_hint: Sign in to open and manage your projects.
projects_empty_body: A project is one architecture, kept on the server: it opens on any machine you sign in from, keeps its history, and is the thing you share with your team or hand to an agent.
projects_empty_point_1: Draw the systems you already run — the sample model is there to borrow from.
projects_empty_point_2: Every change is versioned, so nothing is lost by trying something.
projects_empty_point_3: Share it by link, or connect Cursor and Claude over MCP.
landing_nav_all_integrations_hint: Everything Viaduct talks to, on one page
integrations_title: Connect Viaduct to what you already run
integrations_intro: The model is only worth keeping if the rest of your tooling can read it. Everything below works today — an agent that edits the architecture, an API with a client generator behind it, events when something changes, and files you can take with you.
integrations_top: Four ways the model gets in and out
integrations_all: And the rest of what it speaks
landing_nav_mcp_hint: Cursor and Claude read and write the model
landing_nav_webhooks_hint: Signed events when the model changes
add_person_hint: Person or actor — drawn with the C4 person glyph
landing_shot_hero_alt: Viaduct system context diagram: an internet banking system connected to an external mainframe and an e-mail system
landing_levels_body: Open a system to see its containers, a container to see its components. Every level is a view of the same model, so a rename or a new dependency shows up everywhere it belongs.
landing_levels_alt: Drilling from the system context level into the container level of the same model
landing_tech_body: Pick a technology and the element takes its colour and logo. Datastores are drawn as cylinders, people as actors — so a diagram is scannable before anyone reads a label.
landing_tech_alt: Container diagram with technology-coloured cards for a JavaScript SPA, a mobile app, a Java API and a PostgreSQL datastore
landing_schema_title: The detail that usually lives in another tool
landing_schema_body: Attach an ER schema to a datastore, Markdown documentation to any element, PlantUML sequence diagrams to a service, and API endpoints to a component — all inside the model they describe.
landing_schema_alt: ER schema view of a PostgreSQL container with users, sessions, accounts and transactions tables
landing_cta_title: The sample model is already loaded
landing_cta_body: Open the editor and an Internet Banking system is waiting, modelled across every level, with docs, flows and contracts attached. Clear it when you want to start your own.
landing_tabs_title: Docs, diagrams and schemas live on the element
landing_tab_docs_body: Every element carries its own Markdown pages — a design note on a service, a runbook on a worker, an ADR on a system. Write in the editor with a live preview, insert a stored sequence diagram or an API endpoint as a block, and the page keeps rendering the current version instead of a screenshot that rotted last quarter.
landing_tab_docs_alt: Documentation editor with Markdown on the left and a rendered preview with a table on the right
landing_tab_sequence_body: Design interactions in PlantUML next to a live rendering, with participants checked against the model — a typo in a service name is an error, not a diagram that quietly lies. Diagrams belong to the service they describe and can be embedded in any documentation page.
landing_tab_sequence_alt: Sequence editor with PlantUML source beside the rendered interaction diagram
landing_tab_schema_body: Open a datastore to model its tables, columns and foreign keys. Mark components as API endpoints with method, path and payloads. The detail sits inside the container it belongs to, one double-click from the architecture picture.
landing_tab_schema_alt: ER schema view with users, sessions, accounts and transactions tables joined by foreign keys
landing_flows_title: A request, played back across the canvas
landing_flows_body: A Magic flow is an ordered walk through the model: each step names a hop, the elements it goes from and to, and the connection it uses. Steps that happen at the same time share a stage, so a fan-out reads as a fan-out.
landing_flows_point_1: Build a flow from the elements you already modelled — no second diagram to maintain.
landing_flows_point_2: Play it on the canvas: everything dims except the current hop, and the camera follows the request.
landing_flows_point_3: Generate a sequence diagram from the flow, and attach the docs and diagrams that explain each step.
landing_flows_editor_alt: Magic flow editor listing flows, their ordered steps and the properties of one hop
landing_flows_player_alt: The Magic flow player stepping through a payment: each hop lights up on the diagram while the rest dims
landing_flows_player_caption: Playing “Payment leaves the bank”, step by step.
landing_ai_title: One server, one token, the whole architecture
landing_ai_body: Cursor, Claude Code, Claude Desktop and any other MCP client can read the architecture straight from Viaduct: systems and services, API endpoints with their contracts, WebSocket channels, documentation and sequence diagrams. One hosted MCP server, one personal token, no repository to clone.
landing_ai_point_1: Your agent answers “what talks to what, and over which contract?” from the model instead of guessing from the codebase.
landing_ai_point_2: It can write back too — new services, endpoints, connections and docs land in the same model your team reads.
landing_ai_point_3: Hand it a change set: a piece of work pinned to a fixed version, with the constraints and acceptance criteria it has to prove.
landing_ai_change_sets_title: Work an agent can finish, and you can verify
landing_ai_change_sets_body: A change set is scoped to one pinned version, so nothing shifts under the agent while it builds. It reports each finished piece with the criterion it proves and the commit that proves it — the status moves itself from draft to done, live on your screen.
landing_ai_shot_alt: Change set catalog: work by status, with acceptance criteria and the commits an agent reported against them
landing_design_title: Your designers already use Figma. Now the model does.
landing_design_body: Connect a Figma account in settings and the frames your interface is drawn in become part of the architecture: components point at real nodes, and the values they are allowed to use are read from the file rather than retyped. Nothing is written back, and no picture is copied here.
landing_design_point_1_title: It tells you when the design moved
landing_design_point_1: Work is pinned to the file as it was. When somebody edits the frame afterwards, the change set says which components are now behind — instead of that turning up in review.
landing_design_point_2: The colours, spacing and type in the file come in by name. A component may use those, and a value that is not among them is flagged rather than quietly shipped.
landing_design_point_3_title: Your coding agent gets it too
landing_design_point_3: Everything here rides along in what an agent reads over MCP — the frame, its states, the palette. It builds the loading and error states because they were written down, not because someone remembered.
landing_assist_title: The boring half of documenting, done for you
landing_assist_body: Not every team keeps an agent of their own, and the parts of a model that go undocumented are the dull ones: descriptions nobody wrote, flow steps still called "Step 4". Viaduct's built-in assistant writes those. It is in the editor, it needs no key and no setup, and it never changes your model on its own — every suggestion is shown, and applying it is a button you press.
landing_assist_point_1: A description for any element that lacks one — one at a time, or every blank in a system at once.
landing_assist_point_2: A review of the whole model: what is undescribed, what nothing talks to, what looks like the same job done twice. Every finding names a real element, and clicking it takes you there.
landing_assist_point_3: Names for the steps of a Magic flow that nobody got round to naming — written into the draft, so saving is accepting.
landing_assist_footnote: Included with an account, with a monthly allowance per person. Guests draw; the assistant needs a sign-in.
landing_assist_sample_caption: A review, as it comes back
landing_assist_sample_1: No description — nothing says what it is responsible for, and three services depend on it.
landing_assist_sample_2: Nothing connects to it and it connects to nothing; either the flow is missing or the service is.
landing_assist_sample_3: Appears to do the same job as Billing Service — one of the two is probably the old one.

branch_new_hint: A branch is a full copy of the project you can edit without touching it. It starts from a named version, and comes back through a merge.
branch_intro: Fork the project, try something out, then merge it back. What both sides changed independently is merged for you; what they changed the same way is brought to you as a decision.
branch_state_merged: This branch has been merged into the project.
branch_merge_failed: The merge could not be completed.
branch_preview_failed: The merge could not be computed.
branch_trunk_moved: The project changed while you were reviewing. The merge was recomputed — check it again before merging.
branch_fast_forward: The project has not changed since this branch was created.
branch_diverged: The project has changed since this branch was created.
branch_no_conflicts: Nothing to decide — this branch merges cleanly.
branch_conflict_field: Both sides changed this. Pick the one to keep.
branch_conflict_deleted_trunk: The project deleted this while the branch was still working on it.
branch_conflict_deleted_branch: The branch deleted this while the project was still working on it.
branch_conflict_order: Both sides reordered these steps. Order is meaning in a flow, so pick one.
branch_conflict_dangling: The branch still points at it — “{{owner}}”, {{detail}}. Bring it back, or drop that one reference and leave the rest of the merge as it is.
branch_abandon_confirm: "{{name}}" stays readable in the list, but can no longer be merged.
branch_delete_confirm: “{{name}}” and everything in it is removed for good. Anything not merged is lost.
navigator_protect_trunk_hint: The diagram becomes read-only for everyone, including you. Changes go into a branch and arrive by merge.
navigator_merge_approvals_hint: How many people from the reviewer pool must approve before a branch can merge. 0 turns the gate off.
navigator_merge_reviewers_unshared: Share the project with a GitLab group or user first — reviewers come from the people it is shared with.
navigator_merge_reviewers_hint: People from GitLab groups this project is shared with. Any of them can approve a merge. Requires GitLab sign-in.
navigator_merge_reviewers_empty: No reviewers yet — search to add people.
branch_review_pool_empty: No reviewers in the pool yet — the project owner adds them in settings.
branch_review_blocked_author: You created this branch, so someone else has to approve it.
branch_review_blocked_not_a_reviewer: You are not in the reviewer pool for this project.
branch_from_version_drift: The project has changes that are not in any version yet. They stay on the project — the branch starts from the version above.
branch_needs_version: This project has no named versions yet. Pin one first: a branch starts from an agreed state, and the fork point has to survive — unnamed snapshots are cleared out over time.
branch_conflicts_hint: The merge waits until each of these is answered. Open one to decide it.
branch_conflict_author_only: Only {{name}} can decide these — they created this branch.
branch_resolutions_author_only: Only the person who created this branch can decide its conflicts.
navigator_branch_pattern_hint: Branches must match this pattern when they are created.
branch_name_pattern_mismatch: This project requires a different name format.
branch_blocked_access: You have read access to this project.
